measurement.happened:
This week in Ukraine was dominated by the resumption of peace talks after a nine-month silence, a provocative US territorial proposal, a satellite-internet controversy, and a brutal exchange of strikes on infrastructure. Let me walk through each theme.

PEACE TALKS AND THE DONBAS-FOR-NATO PROPOSAL. The single biggest story of the week is the US-brokered round of Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, held November 9-11, the first in nine months. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner mediated. The talks ended with an agreement on what Kushner called the 'largest prisoner exchange' of the war, but no breakthrough on territory or a ceasefire. Russia and Ukraine discussed a post-war European security framework, ceasefire monitoring, and territory. Then, on November 14, Zelensky dropped a bombshell: the US had floated the idea that Ukraine could cede the Donbas to Russia in exchange for guaranteed NATO membership. Zelensky said he was ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum. He also warned that Ukraine is 'not real estate' and that the new European security framework floated by the US could benefit Putin. Trump said the US is seeing a 'strong inclination' to end the war. Rubio said Ukraine must never again feel threatened. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

EUROPEAN PARTICIPATION AND INTERNAL SQUABBLING. A major sub-thread was Europe trying to get a seat at the table. The EU settled on a five-nation group of national security aides to represent Europe in future talks. There was visible internal tension: Germany's Merz demanded all EU states back Ukraine and was accused of 'blackmail' by Slovak PM Fico over linking Ukraine funding to the EU budget. Berlin and Paris initially temporized on who to send. Russia initially resisted European participation, then Putin let Europe join if they showed 'readiness to contribute.' Zelensky welcomed the prospect. Kushner said the US cannot reach a deal without Europe. The EU also agreed to present a new Russia sanctions package and Ukraine funding measures by year-end. Canada and the EU launched a new alliance covering Ukraine, minerals, and AI. (Sources: Reuters, AP, DW, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

STARLINK AND STARSHIELD CONTROVERSY. This was a recurring and increasingly bitter thread. Zelensky said Starshield speed limits were imposed again, hampering Ukraine's frontline defenses. He escalated his criticism of SpaceX. Democratic US senators ordered Elon Musk to preserve all records on Ukraine Starlink access. BT in the UK held off its Starlink launch until the Ukraine 'noise' died down. Ukraine's military said Starlink disruptions were recurring. This is becoming a political issue inside the US, not just a technical one. (Sources: Reuters, AP, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, TV5Monde.)

RUSSIAN STRIKES ON UKRAINE'S INFRASTRUCTURE. Russia launched a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military factories, hit energy facilities in eight regions, targeted food factories, and pounded the power grid. Kyiv suffered water shortages. The grid operator reported widespread damage. Ukraine raced to repair power plants before winter. Workers at a devastated power plant refused to leave. BBC joined a unit protecting a front-line city under constant drone threat. A 'horrific' Russian drone strike killed 14 at a train station. Zelensky warned Russia's strikes aim to cut Ukraine in half. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

UKRAINE'S DRONE CAMPAIGN AGAINST RUSSIA. Ukraine launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russia in a single night. It hit a ninth Russian oil refinery since the start of November, including Russia's biggest refinery in Siberia. It struck an oil-pumping station in Samara. A drone attack triggered a fire at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga. A Ukrainian drone hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, prompting Finland to contact Ukraine. Sources say recent Ukrainian attacks have reduced Russia's oil processing capacity by 30 percent. Russia's diesel exports dropped. Russia began rationing petrol. The Russian economy is slowing as Ukrainian attacks damage industry. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, CNBC, TV5Monde.)

US ENVOYS SHUTTLE BETWEEN MOSCOW AND DUBLIN. After the Abu Dhabi talks, Witkoff and Kushner flew to Moscow to meet Putin, then to Dublin to meet Zelensky. Putin was described as inflexible and uncompromising, upping his demands. Zelensky said he was pleased with messages from the US envoys and that progress hinges on the US approach to Russia. Witkoff said progress is being made. A Zelensky-Putin direct meeting still appears unlikely at this stage. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

RUSSIAN CASUALTIES AND THE HUMAN COST. A hacked set of official Russian statistics suggested more than 400,000 Russian troops killed. Al Jazeera reported casualties reaching 450,000. Russia recorded over 11,000 foreign military deaths. Ukraine claimed a record 3,000 Russian casualties in a single day. A mother's campaign for Ukrainian sons captured by Russia was profiled. (Sources: TV5Monde, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, BBC.)

CAR BOMBINGS IN RUSSIA. Two car bombs hit Moscow in two days. One killed a military officer, the other badly injured a former aide to a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM. This looks like a tit-for-tat or intelligence-driven escalation. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, CNN, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

INDIA AND THE BLACK SEA. Zelensky spoke to Modi. India signaled readiness to mediate Black Sea food corridors. India also spoke with both Russia and Ukraine ahead of the talks. (Sources: Reuters, DW, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

DEFENSE TECH AND ECONOMY. Ukrainian drone startup UForce closed a $700 million funding round at a $6 billion valuation. A Ukrainian army unit pioneered drone evacuations and is scaling up. Ireland and Ukraine are considering co-production of unmanned drones. Oil prices dropped more than a dollar on hopes for peace. The EU pushed for more joint borrowing to finance Ukraine. (Sources: Reuters, BBC, Bloomberg, CNBC, FT, Al Jazeera.)

CHERNOBYL AND OTHER SMALLER STORIES. Donors promised half the funding to repair the Chernobyl exclusion-zone arch. In South Africa, police arrested nine then a tenth foreigner over an alleged plan to fight in the war. A 10th suspect was arrested. (Sources: TV5Monde, AP, BBC.)
measurement.expected:
Looking at the week of November 14 to roughly November 21, here is my read, theme by theme.

THE DONBAS-FOR-NATO PROPOSAL WILL DOMINATE. Zelensky's revelation that the US floated ceding the Donbas for NATO membership will be the central political story. I expect Zelensky to consult his cabinet and possibly hint at or schedule a referendum on the deal. His own words - that he is ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum - suggest this is not just a talking point. The Ukrainian opposition and pro-Russian politicians in Moscow will both react sharply. Putin will likely use the proposal to pressure Kyiv while publicly downplaying it. I rate this as almost certain to be the dominant headline cluster of the week. (Confidence: almost certain.)

SECOND ROUND OF TALKS OR PREPARATORY MEETINGS. The Abu Dhabi round ended with a prisoner exchange and agreement to continue. The five-nation European delegation will need to be briefed and prepared. I expect either a second round of trilateral talks (possibly in the same or a different venue) or at least a series of preparatory bilateral meetings between US envoys and both sides, with the European team joining. Russia will likely test the European delegation's resolve. I rate a second formal round as probable, and preparatory meetings as almost certain. (Confidence: probable for a second round, almost certain for preparatory contacts.)

PRISONER EXCHANGE LOGISTICS. The 'largest prisoner exchange' was agreed in principle. The actual swap - counting bodies, verifying identities, arranging transport - takes time. I expect the first wave of prisoners to be exchanged within this window, with some bureaucratic friction and possibly a small public ceremony. (Confidence: probable that at least the first batch moves.)

RUSSIAN STRIKES ON ENERGY AND WINTER BLACKOUTS. Russia has been systematically hitting power plants, substations, and water infrastructure. November is the start of real winter. Ukraine's grid is already under stress. I expect continued and possibly intensified Russian strikes on energy and water infrastructure, with more blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Ukraine will keep racing to repair. The 'toughest winter' framing from AP will become a daily reality. (Confidence: almost certain.)

UKRAINE'S DRONE STRIKES ON RUSSIAN OIL. Ukraine has hit nine refineries in November and cut Russian oil processing capacity by 30 percent. Russia is rationing petrol. I expect Ukraine to continue and possibly expand its campaign against Russian refineries, pipelines, and storage, especially as the economic pain becomes more visible domestically in Russia. There may be a new high-profile strike on a major refinery or a pipeline terminal. (Confidence: probable.)

STARLINK AND STARSHIELD CONTROVERSY ESCALATES. Zelensky has now publicly escalated. Democratic senators have ordered Musk to preserve records. BT is holding off its launch. I expect Musk or SpaceX to respond publicly, possibly with a technical explanation or a counter-accusation. The US government may intervene to clarify the rules. There is a real chance this becomes a small political firestorm in Washington, with hearings or a formal letter. (Confidence: probable that the controversy intensifies or at least continues to generate headlines.)

EU BUDGET AND FUNDING FIGHT. Merz's 'blackmail' accusation from Fico and the EU's plan to present new sanctions and Ukraine funding measures by year-end mean the budget clash will continue. I expect more public sparring between Germany and smaller eastern EU states, and a draft funding package to be tabled. (Confidence: probable.)

BALTIC AND MARITIME TENSION. The Ukrainian drone hit on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, Finland's contact with Ukraine, and Baltic drone warnings suggest the maritime front is heating up. I expect at least one more incident in the Baltic or Black Sea, possibly a Russian warship or patrol vessel being targeted or a drone alert in a Baltic state. (Confidence: possible.)

RUSSIAN DOMESTIC PRESSURE. With 400,000-450,000 casualties, petrol rationing, refinery damage, and two car bombs in Moscow, the domestic cost of the war is becoming harder to hide. I expect more visible public frustration in Russia, possibly small protests or a more aggressive information campaign. The car bombings may prompt a visible security crackdown. (Confidence: possible.)

INDIA'S BLACK SEA CORRIDOR PUSH. Zelensky and Modi spoke. India is positioning itself. I expect some concrete proposal or at least a joint statement on Black Sea grain and food corridors. (Confidence: possible.)

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES. Zelensky calling a snap referendum on the NATO-Donbas deal within this week (possible but rushed). A direct Zelensky-Putin meeting (unlikely but not impossible if momentum builds). Russia accepting the five-nation European team and showing up to talks within the week (possible). A major Ukrainian ground offensive or a Russian breakthrough on the front (possible but not the main story). A new round of EU sanctions being formally adopted (possible if the budget fight resolves quickly).

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON. A full ceasefire or a signed peace deal by November 21 (too fast, too many unresolved issues). Zelensky resigning or a major cabinet reshuffle (no signs of it). Russia launching a full-scale new offensive on a new axis (they are focused on the existing front and infrastructure). A major nuclear incident at Chernobyl (the arch repair is ongoing but no signs of crisis). Ukraine joining NATO formally (the proposal is about a security framework, not immediate membership). A warship sinking in the Baltic (the hit on the warship was likely a drone graze, not a sinking).
emoji_reasons: The resumption of US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the Donbas-for-NATO proposal, and the push to include Europe in negotiations made diplomacy the defining story of the week.

Russia pounded Ukraine's power grid, water supply, and military factories while Ukraine hit nine Russian refineries and a warship, making the exchange of strikes on infrastructure the constant backdrop.

The Starlink and Starshield speed-limit controversy, Zelensky's public escalation against SpaceX, and the US congressional order for Musk to preserve records turned a satellite-internet issue into a major political and military story.

delta.motion:
Comparing the two photographs five days apart, the most dramatic growth is in the peace-talks thread. On November 9 it was still in the preparation stage: delegations confirmed, Melania hosting, Trump calling the prospective deal 'big and beautiful.' By November 14 the talks had actually happened (November 9-11 in Abu Dhabi), produced the largest prisoner exchange of the war, and then exploded into the Donbas-for-NATO revelation that Zelensky dropped on the 14th. The theme went from anticipation to execution to a specific, controversial territorial proposal in five days. That is the single biggest shift.

Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refineries grew sharply. The first photo recorded six refineries hit in a week. The second photo records nearly 1,200 drones launched in a single night, a ninth refinery struck (including Russia's largest in Siberia), a 30 percent reduction in Russian oil-processing capacity, a Baltic port on fire, and a warship hit in the Gulf of Finland. The scale jumped from a steady campaign to what reads like an all-out economic siege.

European involvement grew in a different way. The first photo showed Europe warning about irrelevance, the G7 meeting in Paris, and Meloni criticizing the EU's disjointed approach. The second photo shows the EU having settled on a five-nation security-aid group, Germany's Merz demanding all states back Ukraine, Slovak PM Fico accusing Berlin of blackmail over the EU budget, and Russia going from resisting European participation to accepting it if Europe shows 'readiness to contribute.' The theme moved from anxiety to concrete institutional positioning, but with visible internal friction.

The Starlink/Starshield controversy appeared almost from nothing. In the first photo it was a minor footnote (Russia using its own Starlink). By the second photo Zelensky was publicly escalating his criticism of SpaceX, Democratic senators had ordered Elon Musk to preserve all records on Ukraine's Starlink access, and the British telecom BT had held off its Starlink launch until the 'noise' died down. A technical issue became a political flashpoint in the US within five days.

Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure continued and evolved. The first photo focused on power substations, a bridge, and the deadly aid-center strike in Zaporizhzhia. The second photo shows strikes on military factories, energy facilities in eight regions, food factories, the power grid, and a train station where 14 were killed. Kyiv now has water shortages. The pattern is the same (overnight barrages, energy focus) but the targets have broadened to include industry and food processing, and the cumulative damage is becoming visible in daily life.

Several themes shrank or vanished. The Kherson ceasefire ending was a specific event in the first photo and is no longer in the news by the second. The Zelensky-mayor blame game over the blackout was a one-off and disappeared. The SBU corruption scandal, prominent on November 9, is barely visible by November 14. The IMF review, launched on the 9th, has faded from the headlines. Melania Trump's role as 'exclusive intermediary' was central in the first photo and is much quieter in the second.

New themes that appeared between the two photos: the Donbas-for-NATO proposal (the biggest new item), two car bombings in Moscow within two days, India signaling readiness to mediate Black Sea food corridors, the US envoys Witkoff and Kushner physically shuttling to Moscow and then Dublin, the UForce drone startup closing a 700-million-dollar round at a 6-billion valuation, and the Canadian-EU alliance covering Ukraine, minerals, and AI. The car bombings in particular are new: the first photo had no mention of car bombs on Russian soil.

The overall speed of change is fast. The diplomatic track moved from preparation to talks to a specific territorial proposal in five days. The economic-war track went from six refineries to nine and a 30 percent capacity hit. The Starlink issue went from footnote to congressional order. These are not slow drifts; they are step-changes compressed into a weekend and a few working days.
delta.wind:
Abu Dhabi talks. Expected: almost certain to happen, probable to produce a tangible document, possible but not probable to produce a full ceasefire. Reality: the talks happened on schedule. They produced the largest prisoner exchange of the war, which counts as a tangible outcome but is narrower than the 'framework document' I predicted. No full ceasefire, as expected. What I got wrong: the talks themselves did not produce the Donbas-for-NATO proposal. That came on November 14, after the talks, as a revelation by Zelensky about what the US had floated. I expected the talks to center on 'security guarantees and the scope of any ceasefire.' They did, but the specific shape of the US position (cede Donbas, get NATO) was more concrete and more provocative than my 'friction over security guarantees' framing suggested. The talks also produced a post-war European security framework discussion and a ceasefire-monitoring conversation, which I did not specifically predict.

Russian strikes on energy. Expected: almost certain, at least one major overnight barrage, hundreds of thousands without power. Reality: fully confirmed and then some. The overnight strike hit military factories, energy in eight regions, food factories, and the grid. Kyiv had water shortages. Fourteen people were killed at a train station. Workers at a devastated power plant refused to leave. This came true exactly as predicted, maybe slightly more broadly in target types (food factories, military plants) than I specified.

Ukraine's refinery campaign. Expected: probable, at least one or two more strikes on refineries or logistics. Reality: massively exceeded expectations. Nearly 1,200 drones in one night, the ninth refinery of November, Russia's largest refinery in Siberia hit, an oil-pumping station in Samara struck, the Baltic port of Ust-Luga on fire, a warship hit in the Gulf of Finland, and a reported 30 percent reduction in Russian oil-processing capacity. I said 'one or two more strikes.' It was closer to a sustained campaign with a dramatic nighttime surge. I underestimated the tempo and the geographic spread.

Post-talks diplomatic scramble. Expected: almost certain, a flurry of statements from Trump, Zelensky, Putin, Meloni, Merz, Kallas. Reality: yes, but more substantive than a 'flurry of statements.' The US envoys physically traveled to Moscow and Dublin. The EU settled on a five-nation security group. Merz and Fico had a public spat over the EU budget. Russia went from resisting to accepting European participation. The Donbas-for-NATO proposal was revealed. Trump said the US sees a 'strong inclination' to end the war. Rubio said Ukraine must never again feel threatened. This was more than statements; it was institutional positioning and a specific policy proposal. I was right that it would be active but wrong about the form.

IMF review. Expected: probable that the review is underway, almost certain not concluded. Reality: the IMF is barely mentioned in the second photo. The review is presumably ongoing but has not generated headlines. I overestimated its news salience for this specific week. The process is moving, but it is not a driver of this week's story.

Winter heating crisis. Expected: probable, growing complaints, possible rationing, public appeals. Reality: confirmed. Kyiv water shortages, grid operator reporting widespread damage, Ukraine racing to repair before winter, workers refusing to leave a devastated plant. The crisis is real and visible. I was right.

Cyber incidents. Expected: possible, at least one more notable incident. Reality: the 400,000-casualty figure is still circulating (now 450,000 per Al Jazeera), but the alert-app hacking and fake nuclear warnings are no longer prominent. The cyber thread has faded somewhat as a standalone news item, though the casualty-data leak persists. Partially true, but less active than expected.

European military preparation. Expected: probable that exercises continue, unlikely a full deployment decision. Reality: the multinational exercise is not specifically mentioned in the second photo. Instead, the European thread is dominated by the five-nation security group, the Merz-Fico budget fight, and the Canada-EU alliance. The military-exercise angle has been overtaken by the diplomatic-institutional angle. I was right that groundwork is being laid but wrong about the specific form it takes this week.

Domestic political friction. Expected: possible, one more spat or minor reshuffle. Reality: the SBU corruption scandal and the Zelensky-mayor blame game are much quieter in the second photo. The domestic friction has not escalated as I tentatively predicted. It has receded from the headlines. I was too pessimistic (or too attentive to a one-off) about this thread.

US congressional dynamics. Expected: probable, new Congress makes noise, possibly about Patriot systems. Reality: yes, but in a different form. Democratic senators ordered Elon Musk to preserve all records on Ukraine's Starlink access. This is the new Congress acting, but on Starlink rather than on Patriot systems or a structured aid package. I was right that the Congress would be active but wrong about the specific issue.

Things that came that were not expected: the Donbas-for-NATO proposal was the biggest surprise. I expected 'security guarantees' to be discussed but not a specific territorial concession tied to NATO membership. The two car bombings in Moscow in two days were not in my 'less likely surprises' list (I had a Ukrainian drone or missile strike on a Russian capital, which is different from car bombs). India's mediation role on Black Sea food corridors was not mentioned at all in my expectations. The Starlink controversy escalating to a US congressional order was not anticipated. The UForce 700-million-dollar funding round and the Ireland-Ukraine drone co-production were not expected. The warship hit in the Gulf of Finland, prompting Finland to contact Ukraine, was not in my list.

What this says about how our expectations have been wrong for Ukraine: the main pattern is underestimating the specificity and boldness of the US diplomatic position. I expected a framework discussion on security guarantees. The US actually proposed a concrete territorial trade (Donbas for NATO). The second pattern is underestimating the tempo of Ukraine's economic-war campaign. I said 'one or two more strikes.' It was a 1,200-drone night and a 30 percent capacity hit. The third pattern is overestimating the salience of slower-moving institutional processes (IMF review, military exercises) and underestimating the speed at which technical issues (Starlink) become political flashpoints. The fourth pattern is underestimating the role of third parties (India, Canada) and intra-European friction (Merz-Fico) as independent news drivers. In short, my expectations were too institutional and too gradual. The actual week was more dramatic, more specific, and more multi-actor than I modeled.
delta.driver: The force pushing Ukraine from the first photograph to the second is the collision between American urgency to close the war and the gap between what Russia wants on the ground and what Ukraine will accept in exchange. The US midterms are done, the new Democratic Congress is seated and already acting, and Trump wants a 'big and beautiful' deal before the political window shifts again. That urgency is translating into a specific, provocative proposal (cede the Donbas, get NATO) that neither side has fully accepted but both are now negotiating around. At the same time, both belligerents are using maximum kinetic pressure as leverage in the same window: Russia is hitting energy, food, and military industry to make Ukraine feel the winter and the war before it signs, and Ukraine is hitting refineries, ports, and a warship to make Russia feel the economic squeeze before it negotiates from strength. The Starlink controversy is the clearest symptom of this collision: the US controls a critical piece of Ukraine's warfighting infrastructure, and both the political pressure to close the deal and the military pressure to keep fighting are now being fought over satellite bandwidth. Europe is trying to insert itself into this three-way pressure before it is sidelined, which adds a fourth vector of influence (and friction) to an already crowded diplomatic space. The net effect is that five days of headlines in Ukraine are driven less by any single battlefield event than by the accelerating convergence of a US-deadline, a Russian territorial demand, a Ukrainian security demand, and a European institutional anxiety, all compressing into the same short window.

crystal.reasoning:
I start from the present: the Donbas-for-NATO proposal was dropped on Saturday, November 14, the very first day of the forecast window. Zelensky said he is ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum. The US envoys are still in transit between Moscow and Dublin. Russia has just hit energy, food, and military industry in eight regions. Ukraine just launched 1,200 drones and hit a ninth refinery. Starlink has gone from technical footnote to a US congressional order. The EU has a five-nation group but is still squabbling. India is circling the Black Sea. Two car bombs hit Moscow in two days. This is a week that opens at maximum diplomatic and kinetic tension.

The motion tells me the diplomatic track is accelerating, not decelerating. Five days ago the talks were in preparation; now they are in the 'specific proposal being debated' phase. The next logical step is not another round of talks but the reaction to the proposal: who accepts, who rejects, who conditions, who threatens to walk. The motion also shows Ukraine's economic-war tempo is climbing, not plateauing. Nine refineries in a month, 30 percent capacity loss, a warship hit, a Baltic port on fire. The next week will likely see the campaign continue at that tempo or higher, because Ukraine has momentum and Russia has not yet shown a visible counter to the drone swarm. The Starlink thread is in its escalation phase: it went from footnote to congressional order in five days. The next step is either a partial resolution (Musk restores access with conditions) or a further political escalation (a hearing, a formal inquiry, a US government position). The European thread is in its 'institutional positioning' phase: the five-nation group exists on paper, the Merz-Fico budget fight is live, the sanctions package is being drafted. The next step is the first real coordination meeting and the first public disagreement about scope.

The wind tells me I have been wrong in four specific ways, and I must correct. First, I underweight the specificity and boldness of the US position. I should not say 'the US will press for security guarantees.' I should say 'the US will push the Donbas-for-NATO trade as a concrete package and demand a yes-or-no response.' Second, I underweight the tempo of Ukraine's economic war. I should not say 'one or two more refinery strikes.' I should expect the 1,200-drone night to be the new baseline, not the peak. Third, I overweight slow institutional processes. The IMF review, the EU sanctions drafting, the five-nation group's first meeting are real but will not be the headline. The headline will be the referendum debate, the next Russian barrage, and the next Ukrainian drone night. Fourth, I underweight third parties and technical-to-political escalation. India will do something concrete on the Black Sea. Starlink will generate a specific US political event, not just 'more discussion.' The Merz-Fico fight will produce a specific budget consequence, not just 'tension.'

The driver is the same as last week but compressed: the US wants a deal before the political window shifts, Russia wants to extract maximum territory before the winter makes Ukraine desperate, Ukraine wants to hit Russia's economy hard enough that Russia negotiates from weakness, and Europe wants a seat before it is written out. The referendum idea is the new accelerant: it gives Zelensky a way to accept the Donbas concession without looking like he is giving it away, but it also gives every Ukrainian opposition faction, every pro-war general, and every European leader a reason to either support or attack the proposal within days. That is what will drive the news cycle this week.

What I would not bet on: a Zelensky-Putin face-to-face meeting (the shuttle diplomacy is not ready for that), a full ceasefire (the kinetic pressure is too high and the proposal too fresh), a major Ukrainian ground offensive (the energy crisis is consuming resources), a Russian nuclear statement (no trigger), a Ukrainian government reshuffle (the referendum debate will absorb domestic politics), a formal US congressional vote on a new aid package (the Starlink fight is eating the Congress's bandwidth), a new front opening in the Black Sea with a naval engagement (India and Turkey are mediating, not fighting), and a major cyberattack of the alert-app scale (the novelty has worn off).
crystal.forecast:
THE DONBAS-FOR-NATO REFERENDUM DEBATE. This will dominate the week. Zelensky dropped the proposal on Saturday; Monday through Friday will be consumed by reactions. I expect Zelensky to clarify the referendum's scope and timing, likely framing it as a 30-to-60-day process that would cover both the territorial concession and the NATO membership guarantee as a single package. The Ukrainian opposition, particularly the pro-war factions and the regional governors of Donbas oblasts, will mobilize within 48 hours, calling the referendum either a premature capitulation or a necessary test of the nation's will. Russia will issue a statement welcoming the 'pragmatic approach' while quietly demanding that the referendum also cover the status of the Crimean peninsula and the language of the NATO guarantee. Trump will make at least one public statement urging both sides to say yes before the winter deepens. The European five-nation group will issue a joint statement, likely split between those who love the NATO part and those who worry the territorial concession sets a precedent. I am confident this will be the single biggest story of the week. The less-likely surprise the motion makes more probable: Zelensky actually setting a specific date for the referendum, say mid-December, which would force all other threads to organize around that deadline.

RUSSIAN KINETIC ESCALATION AND WINTER PRESSURE. Russia will launch at least one more major overnight barrage, and the pattern will continue to broaden. Last week the targets were energy, food factories, military plants, and a train station. I expect this week to see strikes on water infrastructure (Kyiv already has shortages), possibly a chemical or pharmaceutical plant, and at least one strike on a railway hub or a bridge that was not hit last week. The winter heating crisis will worsen: I expect at least one major city to report a full-day power outage, public queues for heating fuel, and Zelensky making a direct appeal to the population to conserve. The less-likely surprise: a Russian strike that hits a major hospital or a school, generating a new wave of international outrage and possibly a UN Security Council emergency session. I would not bet on a Russian ground offensive in this window; the kinetic pressure is coming from the air, not the front.

UKRAINE'S DRONE AND ECONOMIC CAMPAIGN. The 1,200-drone night and the 30 percent capacity reduction are the new baseline, not the peak. I expect Ukraine to hit at least one more refinery or oil-processing facility, and to expand the target set to include a second warship or a naval base in the Black Sea or the Baltic. The Samara pumping station and the Ust-Luga port fire suggest Ukraine is hitting the logistics chain, not just the processing plants. I expect a strike on a major railway junction or a pipeline terminal. Russia's petrol rationing will spread to at least two more regions. The less-likely surprise: a Ukrainian drone or missile hitting a target inside Moscow or St. Petersburg, not just the suburbs, which would be a step up in the tit-for-tat escalation that the car bombings have set in motion. I am moderately confident in the continued refinery campaign and the expansion to logistics; less confident in a Moscow-centre hit, but the car-bomb pattern makes it more probable than it looks.

STARLINK AND THE US POLITICAL BATTLE. The congressional order to preserve records is the floor, not the ceiling. I expect at least one of three things: a formal hearing or subcommittee session where Musk or a SpaceX executive is questioned, a US State Department or Pentagon statement clarifying the government's position on Ukraine's Starlink access, or a partial restoration of Starlink service with new conditions that Zelensky publicly accepts or rejects. The British BT launch decision will be revisited, either going ahead or being delayed again. Fire Point and other Ukrainian alternatives will get a new funding announcement or a government contract. The less-likely surprise: a Republican senator or the White House itself taking a public position, which would turn the Starlink issue from a Democratic-leaned congressional fight into a broader US political story. I am confident the Starlink thread will generate at least one major news event this week; the specific form is uncertain.

EUROPEAN INSTITUTIONAL POSITIONING AND THE MERZ-FICO FIGHT. The five-nation security group will hold its first coordination meeting or produce its first joint position paper. The Merz-Fico budget fight will either produce a specific compromise (Ukraine funding linked to a timeline) or a public deadlock that stalls the EU sanctions package. The new Russia sanctions package will be in its drafting or voting stage, with at least one member state (likely Hungary or Slovakia) pushing for a watered-down version. The Canada-EU alliance will produce a concrete first deliverable, possibly a joint statement on mineral supply chains or a specific AI collaboration project. I am moderately confident in the five-nation group producing something visible; less confident in the sanctions package being finalized, because the Merz-Fico fight is a real obstacle.

US ENVOY SHUTTLE AND THE PUSH FOR A RESPONSE. Witkoff and Kushner will make at least one more trip to Moscow and one to Kyiv or Dublin. The purpose will be to get Russia and Ukraine to respond to the Donbas-for-NATO proposal. I expect Putin to be described as 'inflexible' or 'studying the proposal' and Zelensky to be described as 'open but demanding guarantees.' A Zelensky-Putin direct phone call is possible but I would not bet on it; the shuttle diplomacy is the preferred channel. Trump will make at least one public statement, likely on social media, expressing optimism or mild frustration. The less-likely surprise: the US envoys presenting a written 'package deal' that bundles the Donbas concession, the NATO guarantee, the ceasefire monitoring mechanism, and the prisoner-exchange framework into a single document, which would be a step beyond last week's 'discussion' phase.

INDIA, THE BLACK SEA, AND THIRD-PARTY MEDIATION. India's signal of readiness to mediate Black Sea food corridors will produce a concrete next step: a joint India-Ukraine-Russia working group, a specific corridor proposal, or a statement from Modi's office. Turkey will be drawn in as the strait authority. I expect at least one grain or fuel shipment to transit the Black Sea under a new or updated framework. The less-likely surprise: India formally proposing to host a follow-up round of talks, which would be a significant shift in the diplomatic geography.

RUSSIAN DOMESTIC PRESSURE: CAR BOMBS, CASUALTIES, AND PUBLIC OPINION. The two car bombs in Moscow in two days will generate a security crackdown and possibly a third incident. Russian authorities will announce a 'major operation' or an arrest wave. The 400,000-to-450,000 casualty figure will continue to circulate, and Russia will either confirm a revised number or release a contradictory figure. I expect at least one Russian regional governor to publicly complain about the war's economic impact, which would be a sign of internal pressure. The less-likely surprise: a visible protest or a low-level official resignation in a Russian city, which would signal that the war's domestic cost is starting to register in public life.

UKRAINIAN DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE REFERENDUM BACKLASH. The referendum idea will trigger internal debate. I expect the opposition to hold at least one rally or issue a joint statement, the regional governors of Donetsk and Luhansk to publicly weigh in, and the SBU or the military to issue a statement supporting or questioning the timing. Zelensky's approval ratings will be discussed in the media, and at least one poll will be released. I would not bet on a government reshuffle or a no-confidence motion in this window; the referendum debate will absorb the domestic political energy.

ECONOMY, OIL, AND FINANCE. Oil prices will be volatile: the peace-talks optimism will pull prices down, while the refinery damage and petrol rationing will pull them up. I expect a net decline of 1 to 3 percent over the week, with a spike if a major refinery is hit. Ukraine's sovereign bonds will react to the referendum news: a short-term dip on the territorial-concession fear, followed by a recovery if the NATO guarantee is seen as credible. The EU's joint borrowing mechanism for Ukraine will see a new tranche discussion or a specific allocation. The UForce funding round will be followed by at least one more Ukrainian defense-tech deal or partnership announcement.
crystal.headline: Ukraine Weighs Donbas Referendum as Drone War Intensifies
emoji_reasons: Zelensky's proposal to put the Donbas-for-NATO trade to a public referendum is the single most consequential and new development of the week, reshaping the entire diplomatic and domestic political landscape.

Both sides are escalating kinetic pressure simultaneously: Russia is broadening its strikes to food, water, and military industry, while Ukraine is hitting refineries, ports, and warships at a tempo that is becoming a sustained economic siege.

The Starlink controversy has escalated from a technical dispute to a US congressional order, making satellite internet access a political flashpoint that will generate at least one major news event in the coming days.
crystal.tldr: Next week will be dominated by the fallout from the US Donbas-for-NATO proposal and Zelensky's referendum idea, with both sides and Europe reacting in the first 48 hours. Russia will continue its overnight barrages on energy, water, and food infrastructure as winter deepens, while Ukraine will push its drone campaign against Russian refineries and logistics at the new high tempo. The Starlink dispute will escalate into a specific US political event, and the EU will struggle to present a unified position amid the Merz-Fico budget fight.
crystal.eli5:
Imagine a big argument between three friends about how to split a pizza. One friend (the US) just said, "You can give them a slice of your pizza, but in return, you get to sit at the table at every dinner party forever." The other two friends (Ukraine and Russia) are now arguing about whether that deal is fair. Ukraine's leader said he wants to ask all his friends (the voters) what they think before he agrees. That is the referendum idea. It is the biggest story this week.

At the same time, both sides are still throwing things at each other. Russia is hitting Ukraine's power plants, water pipes, and food factories, trying to make winter really hard so Ukraine will say yes to the deal. Ukraine is sending thousands of small flying robots (drones) at Russia's oil factories, trying to make Russia's gas stations run dry so Russia will also say yes. Both sides are using their strongest moves right now because they think the window to make a deal is closing.

There is also a side-argument about the internet. Ukraine uses a special satellite internet system to talk to its soldiers, and the company that runs it has been slowing it down. Now the US politicians are getting angry and ordering the company to keep all its records. It is like if your school's Wi-Fi kept getting slow during a test, and the principal started asking the internet company for a full report.

Europe is trying to get a seat at the pizza-splitting table, but they are arguing among themselves about who gets to speak for the whole group. India is offering to help fix the delivery route for grain ships in the Black Sea. And in Russia, two car bombs went off in the capital in two days, which makes the government nervous and the public more impatient about the war.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A captured the major structural themes of the week well. It correctly predicted the Abu Dhabi talks would happen (almost certain), that they would produce a tangible document but not a signed peace deal, that Russia would continue striking energy infrastructure, that Ukraine's refinery campaign would continue, and that there would be a post-talks diplomatic scramble. Its prediction of a 'joint communique or framework document' was directionally right but less precise than the actual outcome, which was a specific prisoner exchange agreement framed as the 'largest' of the war. A's 'less likely surprises' section was notably prescient: it flagged a possible strike on Moscow or St. Petersburg (the actual event was car bombs in Moscow, close in spirit but different in mechanism), a minor Black Sea escalation (the actual event was a warship hit in the Gulf of Finland, wrong sea but right idea), and Zelensky making a surprise trip to a Western capital (he went to Dublin). A correctly identified the 400,000-casualty data leak as a cyber story, the G7 in Paris setting the European tone, and the new Democratic Congress making noise about Ukraine. A's prediction that the talks would center on 'security guarantees, the scope of any ceasefire, and whether a broader all-of-Europe deal is on the table' is close to the actual Donbas-for-NATO proposal, though it did not specifically predict a territorial concession in exchange for NATO membership. A missed the Starlink/Starshield speed-limit controversy entirely, which became one of the top five stories of the week with at least a dozen headlines. A also missed the India-Black Sea food corridor angle, the UForce $700 million funding round, and the specific Merz-Fico 'blackmail' fight over EU budget linkage. A's winter heating crisis prediction (hundreds of thousands without power, localized rationing, public appeals) was broadly correct, as was its prediction of continued Ukrainian refinery strikes and the post-talks envoy shuttle. Overall, A painted a competent but somewhat generic picture of the week, hitting the major beats while missing the specific color that made the week distinctive.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B captured the week's dynamics with more nuance and precision. Its central framing of the talks as the 'defining event' through which everything else is read matches the actual reporting structure. B's prediction that the talks would generate 'a headline about a breakthrough that is, in substance, a process agreement' is remarkably close to what happened: the 'largest prisoner exchange' was framed as a breakthrough but was substantively a process agreement with no territorial or ceasefire breakthrough. B's reference to the Oleshky pattern (a locally brokered arrangement that holds briefly then frays) is a good structural insight that matches the fragile, time-limited nature of the prisoner exchange. B correctly predicted the European participation angle, the internal EU squabbling over who to send (the actual Merz-Fico fight, the Berlin-Paris temporizing), and the Kushner 'US cannot reach a deal without Europe' line. B's treatment of the refinery campaign with the nuance of a possible 'brief tactical pause during the talks' is more realistic than A's simpler 'it continues' framing, and the actual reporting shows the campaign continued at high intensity (1,200 drones in one night, ninth refinery, warship hit) with no clear pause. B's cyber section is stronger than A's: it correctly frames the 400,000-death figure as a 'media war' with Russia contesting and Ukraine trying to verify, which matches the actual reporting (Al Jazeera 450,000, Russia's 11,000 foreign deaths, Ukraine's claimed 3,000 in a day). B's congressional dynamics section is more nuanced, correctly noting that the effect is 'more about tone and pressure than concrete legislative action' and that the new Congress will use the talks as 'a test case for its oversight role,' which matches the actual Democratic senators ordering Musk to preserve Starlink records. B's 'not to bet on' list is well-calibrated and mostly accurate: no full peace deal (correct), no major ground offensive (correct), no dramatic congressional vote (correct), no Zelensky resignation (correct), no full EU membership treaty (correct), no Black Sea naval incident (close, but the warship was in the Gulf of Finland, not the Black Sea). B missed the Starlink/Starshield controversy as a major headline story, mentioning Russia's own satellite network but not predicting the Starshield speed-limit dispute becoming a top-five story with BT holding off its launch and Democratic senators issuing a formal order to Musk. B also missed the specific Donbas-for-NATO proposal, though its general framing of 'security guarantees' and 'a narrow operational arrangement' is closer to the actual outcome than A's 'framework document.' B's mention of Melania Trump as a likely presence or reference was not borne out in the reporting. B correctly flagged the Chernobyl arch funding as a smaller concrete item, which did materialize. B's treatment of the US envoys shuttle (Witkoff and Kushner to Moscow then Dublin) is implied in its diplomatic scramble predictions. Overall, B painted a more textured and accurate picture of the week's diplomatic and military dynamics, with better calibration of what would and would not happen.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts are competent and hit the major structural themes: the Abu Dhabi talks, continued Russian energy strikes, Ukraine's refinery campaign, the post-talks diplomatic scramble, the cyber front, and the new Democratic Congress. Neither predicted the Starlink/Starshield controversy as a major story, which is a shared and significant miss given it generated at least a dozen headlines. Neither specifically predicted the Donbas-for-NATO proposal, the single biggest story of the week, though both captured the general direction of security guarantees and territorial questions. B edges ahead on several dimensions. First, B's framing of the talks outcome as 'a breakthrough that is substantively a process agreement' is closer to the actual prisoner-exchange-announced-as-breakthru outcome than A's 'joint communique or framework document.' Second, B's 'not to bet on' list is more useful and more accurate, correctly excluding a full peace deal, a major ground offensive, a Zelensky resignation, and a full EU membership treaty, while A's 'unlikely' list is similar but less precisely calibrated. Third, B's treatment of the cyber front, the congressional dynamics, and the EU internal squabbling is more nuanced and better matches the actual reporting. Fourth, B's structural insight about the Oleshky pattern and the fragility of any concession is a better read on the prisoner exchange outcome. A's strengths include a clearer structured format with explicit confidence levels, a prescient 'less likely surprises' section (car bombing in Moscow, warship, Zelensky surprise trip), and a more specific winter heating crisis prediction. However, A's predictions are somewhat more generic and less textured than B's. A reader using B's forecast would have a better mental model of how the week would unfold, particularly on the diplomatic dynamics, the talks outcome, and the secondary threads. B's extra detail on the Oleshky pattern, the congressional tone, the EU internal fight, and the 'not to bet on' list all paid off. A's extra detail on the winter heating crisis and the G7 European tone also paid off, but to a lesser degree. The shared Starlink miss is a significant gap for both, but B's overall accuracy on the things it did predict gives it the edge. VERDICT: B
